items.title: allenai/HiRO-ACEv2
items.content: # HiRO-ACEv2 The HiRO-ACEv2 framework enables efficient generation of 3 km precipitation, 10 m eastward and northward winds, and sea level pressure fields over decades of simulated climate and arbitrary regions of the globe. HiRO (High Resolution Output) is a diffusion model which generates downscaled fields at 3 km resolution from 100 km resolution inputs. The HiROv2 checkpoint included in this model generates 6-hourly averaged surface precipitation rates at 3 km resolution, and instantaneous 10 m eastward and northward winds and sea level pressure at 6-hour frequency. The Ai2 Climate Emulator (ACE) is a family of models designed to simulate atmospheric variability from the time scale of days to centuries. For usage with the HiROv2 downscaling model, we include a checkpoint for ACE2S-X-SHiELD. For more details, please see the accompanying HiRO-ACEv2 paper linked below. ### Quick links - 📃 [Paper](http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.17693) - 💻 [Code](https://github.com/ai2cm/ace) - 💬 [Docs](https://ai2-climate-emulator.readthedocs.io/en/stable/) - 📂 [All ACE Models](https://huggingface.co/collections/allenai/ace-67327d822f0f0d8e0e5e6ca4) ### Inference quickstart 1. Download this repository. Optionally, you can just download a subset of the `forcing_data` and `initial_conditions` for the period you are interested in. 2. Install code dependencies with `pip install fme`. 3. Update paths in the ACE inference config file `ace2s_inference_config_global.yaml`. Specifically, update `experiment_dir`, `checkpoint_path`, `initial_condition.path` and `forcing_loader.dataset.path`. 4. Update paths in the HiROv2 downscaling inference config file `hiro_downscaling_ace2s_pnw_output.yaml`. Specifically, update `experiment_dir`, `model.checkpoint_path`, and `data.coarse`. The directory path in `data.coarse` should point to the same ACE inference `experiment_dir` from step 3. Optionally, if you wish to change the region and/or time selection of the area(s) to downscale you may edit those in the downscaling config (see [downscaling inference docs](https://ai2-climate-emulator.readthedocs.io/en/latest/downscaling_inference.html) for more details). An example of global downscaling is also provided in `hiro_downscaling_ace2s_global_output.yaml`. 4. Run the script `run-hiro-ace.sh`. ### Strengths and weaknesses #### ACE2S-X-SHiELD The strengths of ACE2S-X-SHiELD are: - stochastic (generative) emulator of 100km coarsened X-SHiELD - improved small scale variability compared to deterministic ACE2 (especially surface precipitation) - exact conservation of global dry air mass and moisture - low time-mean biases for most variables relative to the 10-year training data available - compatible with HiRO model with no observed degradation - similar tropical cyclone generation to X-SHiELD Some known weaknesses of ACE2S-X-SHiELD are: - trained only on 9 years of X-SHiELD (2014-2022) - not expected to generalize outside of the limited forcing conditions used during training (e.g., past/future SSTs and CO2) - may not produce statistically independent and representative samples of the base X-SHiELD model when run for significantly longer than 9 years - not suitable for weather forecasting (e.g., not trained on reanalysis data only climate model output) - model was not tested as rigorously as ACE2-ERA5 (e.g., cannot comment on stratospheric variability, etc) - some aspects of the pre-training and fine-tuning methodologies did not have ablations - exactly pre-training and fine-tuning methodologies are subject to potential significant changes for future versions #### HiROv2 The strengths of HiROv2 are: - Quickly generates surface precipitation rate, 10 m eastward and northward winds, and sea level almost anywhere on the globe analogous to X-SHiELD 3 km output - Reproduces surface precipitation rate, 10 m winds, and sea level pressure distribution of X-SHiELD out to the 99.9999th percentile and generates realistic fields for snapshots of events with high regional impacts (ex. tropical cyclones, downscaled winds, atmospheric rivers) - Low time-mean biases against X-SHiELD - Recovers time-mean characteristics of precipitation related to topography - Stochastic for easy ensemble generation of small-scale variability Some known weaknesses of HiROv2 are: - Not expected to generalize to climates outside of the 10-year training dataset - Only produces precipitation, wind, and pressure features representative of X-SHiELD data, not observations - Not trained or tested outside of 66S -- 70N, and cannot run outside of 88S or 88N - Downscaling regions larger than the 16x16 1-degree patch size used for training will have discontinuities for patch overlaps of 0 or some blending artifacting from averaging in the overlap region for overlaps > 0 ## License This model is licensed under Apache 2.0. It is intended for research and educational use in accordance with Ai2's [Responsible Use Guidelines](https://allenai.org/responsible-use). ## Attribution This model is trained using data processed from X-SHIELD (eXperimental System for High-resolution prediction on Earth-to-Local Domains) provided by the Geophysical Fluid Dynamics Laboratory (GFDL).

## Introduction We're introducing **Ling-3.1-flash**, an upgraded native hybrid reasoning model designed for complex, real-world tasks. With **560B** total parameters, **25B** active parameters per token, and a **1M-token context window**, Ling-3.1-flash builds upon Ling-3.0-flash with improvements in architecture, performance on real-world capabilities. With stronger real-world capabilities, Ling-3.1-flash shows improvements across a range of real-world tasks, including general-purpose agents, search, office productivity, and software engineering. It demonstrates strong performance on benchmarks such as **GDPVal-AA V2.1, HealthBench Professional, FrontierSWE, and Terminal-Bench 4.0**, covering office tasks, healthcare, software engineering, and terminal-based tool use. The model also shows improvements in specialized domains such as finance and materials science. ## Model Overview The model summary information and architecture diagram are as follows: | Architecture | Hybrid-linear MoE | | --- | --- | | Parameter Scale | Total 560B, Activated 25B | | Transformer Layers | 63 KDA + 9 Gated MLA (7:1) | | Number of Dense Layers | 4 | | Number of Routed Experts | 512 | | Number of Shared Experts | 1 | | Number of Activated Experts | 8 | | Attention Heads | 64 | | Hidden Size | 4096 | | Expert Intermediate Size | 1280 | | Dense Intermediate Size | 10240 | | Vocabulary Size | 157184 | ## Evaluation We have conducted a comprehensive evaluation of Ling-3.1-flash across multiple authoritative benchmarks. **Ling-3.1-flash** performs strongly on representative coding/agentic benchmarks including **Terminal-Bench 4.0, SWE-bench Pro, FrontierSWE, GDPVal-AA V2.1, Automationbench, MCP-Atlas**, **SkillsBench, etc**. In practice, Ling-3.1-flash delivers a strong user experience across frameworks including **Claude Code**,** Kilo Code**,** Qwen Code**,** Hermes Agent**,** **and** OpenClaw**, etc. Beyond agentic tasks, Ling-3.1-flash performs strongly on real-world tasks across **STEM, healthcare, and finance**. We also introduce **LingCode**, a harness built on the open-source coding agent Pi, and enhanced to support complex, long-horizon coding tasks that run for hours, involve hundreds of rounds of tool calls, and require repeated context compaction. LingCode delivers significant performance gains on some coding agent tasks, and we are considering open-sourcing it in the future. ## Quickstart #### SGLang (Recommended) The day-0 SGLang image includes Ling-3.1-flash support, MTP (NEXTN) speculative decoding, and the Hopper decode optimizations: ```bash docker pull lmsysorg/sglang:dev-ling-3.1-flash ``` ##### Run Inference **Server** (8x H200, TP8 + EP8): ```bash docker run --gpus all --network host --ipc=host --rm \ lmsysorg/sglang:dev-ling-3.1-flash \ python3 -m sglang.launch_server \ --model-path inclusionAI/Ling-3.1-flash \ --tp 8 --ep 8 \ --speculative-algorithm NEXTN \ --host 0.0.0.0 --port 30000 ``` On 4x GB300, use `--tp 4 --ep 4` instead. Hopper decode optimizations (optional, ~10% faster batch-1 decode) can be enabled with `SGLANG_ENABLE_FP8_BLOCK_GEMV=1` and `SGLANG_ENABLE_FUSED_KDA_OUTPUT_QUANT=1`. **Client** ```bash curl -s http://localhost:30000/v1/chat/completions \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{"model": "Ling-3.1-flash", "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "What is the capital of France?"}], "chat_template_kwargs": {"enable_thinking": true}, "stream": true, "temperature": 1.0, "top_k": 20, "top_p": 0.95}' ``` Verified recipes for H200, GB300, H800, H100, and B200, plus HiCache (Mooncake L3), reasoning on/off, tool calling, and measured accuracy/speed numbers, are in the [SGLang Ling-3.1-flash cookbook](https://docs.sglang.io/cookbook/autoregressive/InclusionAI/Ling-3.1-flash). #### vLLM ##### Environment Preparation ```bash pip install uv uv venv ~/my_ling_env source ~/my_ling_env/bin/activate git clone -b vllm https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm.git cd vllm VLLM_USE_PRECOMPILED=1 uv pip install --editable . --torch-backend=auto ``` #### Run inference **Server** ```bash vllm serve "$MODEL_PATH" \ --port "$PORT" \ --trust-remote-code \ --served-model-name auto \ --tensor-parallel-size 8 \ --gpu-memory-utilization 0.85 \ --enable-prefix-caching \ --enable-expert-parallel \ --mamba-cache-mode align \ --enable-auto-tool-choice \ --tool-call-parser ling3 \ --reasoning-parser ling3 \ --speculative-config '{"method":"mtp","num_speculative_tokens":3}' ``` **Client** It is recommended to use the sampling params (temperature=1.0, top_p=0.95, top_k=20) and turn on enable_thinkingfor better performance. ```bash curl -s http://${MASTER_IP}:${PORT}/v1/chat/completions \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{"model": "auto", "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "What is the capital of France?"}], "chat_template_kwargs": {"enable_thinking": true}, "stream": true, "temperature": 1.0, "top_k": 20, "top_p": 0.95}' ``` ## Training content summary The public training-content summary identifying **Ling-3.1-flash** is available below. Please refer to the document for its covered model versions, training-content scope, summary version, and update date. - [Training-content summary (PDF)](https://huggingface.co/inclusionAI/AI-Transparency/resolve/main/Ling-3.1_TDS-Summary.pdf) - [Training-content documentation index](https://huggingface.co/inclusionAI/AI-Transparency) This summary concerns training-content disclosure; it does not replace the model’s technical documentation, usage terms, or license.

items.title: Build self-improving document processing using Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
items.summary: Learn how to build an agentic intelligent document processing (IDP) system using Amazon Bedrock AgentCore that classifies, extracts, validates, and learns from business documents with minimal human intervention, automatically handling new document formats without manual template configuration.
items.content:
Artificial Intelligence 

 Build self-improving document processing using Amazon Bedrock AgentCore

 IDC research shows that document-related challenges cost organizations $19,732 for each information worker annually and reduce productivity by 21.3 percent. Organizations receiving invoices from hundreds of suppliers often face layouts that vary by issuer and change without notice. Template-based systems require constant maintenance at this scale. Staff can spend up to 30 percent of their time on document-related tasks, and manual data entry error rates range from 1–4 percent . Conventional intelligent document processing (IDP) solutions address some of this burden, but they require extensive upfront configuration for each document format and break when layouts vary across vendors.

 In this post, you learn how to build an agentic IDP system using Amazon Bedrock AgentCore that classifies, extracts, validates, and learns from business documents with minimal human intervention. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with any framework or model. Your agents automatically handle new document formats, such as supplier invoices, purchase orders, insurance claims, and loan applications. By the end of this post, you can:

 Deploy a multi-agent IDP system, often in under 20 minutes.

 Process new document types without manual template configuration.

 Let agents train themselves on each new document format and reuse what they learn, so later documents of that type go straight to extraction without retraining.

 Challenges with rule-based document processing

 Many IDP pipelines require you to define templates, extraction rules, and validation logic for every document format upfront. When a new vendor sends a purchase order with a different layout, the pipeline breaks. This creates three core challenges:

 Template rigidity: Each new document format requires manual configuration, and even minor layout changes can cause extraction failures.

 No learning: The same extraction errors repeat across similar documents because the system doesn’t retain knowledge from previous corrections.

 Scaling burden: Each new vendor or document variant multiplies the maintenance effort, and organizations processing documents from hundreds of sources face ongoing operational costs.

 An agentic approach addresses these challenges. Instead of static templates, AI agents analyze each document, generate extraction instructions, validate results, and learn from corrections automatically. Over time, your system builds a knowledge base of document formats, so you process similar documents with minimal additional configuration.

 Solution overview

 In this solution, eight specialized agents collaborate across two graph-based workflows running on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore.

 The following diagram shows the multi-agent workflow graph built using Strands Agents , an open source SDK for building AI agents.

 Figure 1: Multi-agent orchestration workflow graph

 Identification workflow : The Analyzer agent extracts text using Amazon Textract and identifies the document type and sender. The Matcher agent searches for similar documents using vector similarity in Amazon S3 Vectors , a capability of Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3).

 Training workflow (new document types): When no match is found, the Instructions agent generates extraction prompts, the Extractor agent extracts structured data, and the Validator agent checks results against schemas and business rules in Amazon Aurora DSQL . If validation fails, the Instructions Fixer agent refines the prompts and retries. On success, the Save Instructions agent persists the instructions for reuse.

 Automation workflow (known document types): When a match is found, the Extractor agent uses existing instructions. If validation fails, the Troubleshooter agent fixes the extracted data directly without modifying instructions.

 How it works

 The following diagram shows the infrastructure architecture for the solution.

 Figure 2: Agentic IDP infrastructure architecture on AWS

 Business documents arrive in Amazon Simple Email Service (Amazon SES) or direct upload to Amazon S3.

 Amazon EventBridge triggers an AWS Lambda function that creates a tracking job in Amazon DynamoDB and invokes AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore.

 AgentCore runtime orchestrates document processing through Strands Agents.

 Your agents securely access AWS resources through machine-to-machine credentials managed by AgentCore Identity, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, and Amazon Cognito .

 Your Lambda functions become agent-compatible tools through the Model Context Protocol (MCP) interface of AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore.

 Agents extract text using Amazon Textract, classify documents using vector embeddings in S3 Vectors, and validate data against business rules in Aurora DSQL.

 Agents access enterprise data through MCP servers to validate extracted content against business rules.

 You monitor status and troubleshoot issues through a chat-enabled dashboard hosted on Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS).

 You gain visibility into agent performance through AgentCore Observability, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, and Amazon CloudWatch telemetry.

 Deploy the solution

 Follow these steps to deploy the solution infrastructure and web UI to your AWS account.

 Prerequisites

 To deploy this solution, you must have:

 An AWS account .

 Access to Amazon Bedrock with Amazon Nova and Anthropic (Claude) models enabled. For model availability by AWS Region, refer to Supported models by AWS Region in Amazon Bedrock .

 Access to Amazon Bedrock AgentCore (Runtime, Gateway, Identity), S3 Vectors, and Amazon Aurora DSQL in a supported Region .

 AWS Cloud Development Kit (AWS CDK) v2 installed.

 Docker installed and running (required for building and deploying container images).

 Python 3.11+ and Node.js 18+.

 AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) permissions to create S3 buckets, Lambda functions, DynamoDB tables, Cognito user pools, Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR) repositories, and Amazon ECS services.

 Clone the repository and set up the environment: 

 git clone https://github.com/aws-samples/agenticidp-guidance.git
cd agenticidp-guidance

uv venv
source .venv/bin/activate
uv pip install -r requirements.txt

cd ui/orchestrator
npm install
cd ../.. 

 Deploy the stacks: 

 uv run deploy.py --admin-email your-email@example.com 

 This deploys six AWS CloudFormation stacks: Core (S3, Cognito, DynamoDB), Gateway (Lambda tools, AgentCore Gateway), Aurora (Amazon Aurora DSQL), Agent (AgentCore runtime, containers), UI Orchestrator (API endpoints), and Modern UI (React app on Amazon CloudFront ). Deployment takes approximately 15–20 minutes.

 Verify deployment by checking that each stack shows CREATE_COMPLETE in the CloudFormation console.

 Process files and review results

 After deployment, you receive an email with the CloudFront URL, username, and temporary password.

 Process a document

 Sign in to the web UI and choose Process Document .

 Upload a sample purchase order from infrastructure/sample_data/purchase_orders/training/ .

 The document enters the agent workflow: 

 The Analyzer agent extracts text and identifies the sender and document type.

 The Matcher agent searches for similar documents in the vector store.

 For a new document type, the training workflow generates extraction instructions, extracts data, validates it, and saves the instructions for future use.

 For a known document type, the automation workflow extracts data using existing instructions and validates it.

 Review results in the Review Jobs and Instructions tab to verify extracted data, validation results, and generated instructions.

 Example: A new document type (training workflow)

 Suppose you upload the first purchase order from a new retailer, Two Wheel Store. The Matcher agent searches the vector store, finds no similar document, and routes the job through the training workflow.

 The Analyzer agent uses Amazon Textract to extract the raw document text:

 # PURCHASE ORDER
FROM: Two Wheel Store
Order #: PO-2026-0102-2584
Date: 2026-01-02

## Items Ordered
AC-021 Advanced Computer Qty: 1 $75.61
 Colors: cr4321 @ $75.61
...
SB-004 Folding Classic Qty: 8 $9634.32
 Colors: cb8901 I Sizes: S @ $1204.29

TOTAL: $14931.54 

 The Instructions agent generates extraction prompts from the schema, and the Extractor agent produces structured JSON:

 {
 "po_number": "PO-2026-0102-2584",
 "retailer_name": "Two Wheel Store",
 "order_date": "2026-01-02T00:00:00Z",
 "line_items": [
 { "sku": "AC-021", "product_name": "Advanced Computer", "quantity": 1, "unit_price": 75.61, "line_total": 75.61 },
 { "sku": "SB-004", "product_name": "Folding Classic", "quantity": 8, "unit_price": 1204.29, "line_total": 9634.32 }
 ],
 "order_total": 14931.54
} 

 The Validator agent checks the result against the schema and fails :

 validation_status: INVALID
error: 'SB-004' does not match '^AB-[A-Z]{2}-\d{3}$' 

 The vendor’s SKU format ( SB-004 ) doesn’t match Acme Bikes’ internal format ( AB-SB-004 ). The Instructions Fixer agent diagnoses the mismatch and adds an explicit SKU transformation rule to the extraction prompt: prefix vendor SKUs with AB- . On the second pass, the seven line items validate successfully, and the Save Instructions agent persists the refined prompt to the vector store. End-to-end time for this first run: 3 minutes 49 seconds.

 Example: A known document type (automation workflow)

 When a second purchase order from Two Wheel Store arrives, the Matcher agent finds the stored instructions from the first run with a confidence score of 3.946 (threshold: 3.7) and routes the job through the automation workflow:

 The Extractor agent applies the stored instructions directly, so the orchestrator skips prompt

items.title: Generate presentations with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
items.summary: This post walks you through building an AI agent system with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore that automates PowerPoint presentation creation from enterprise documents. A supervisor agent, Retrieval Augmented Generation, and Amazon Bedrock Guardrails generate grounded presentations in under 90 seconds.
items.content:
Artificial Intelligence 

 Generate presentations with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore

 A financial services team spends significant time each week manually creating client PowerPoint presentations from quarterly reports, compliance documents, and market analyses. Each presentation requires reading hundreds of pages, extracting key data points, structuring slides, and generating supporting visuals. This post walks you through building an AI agent system using Amazon Bedrock AgentCore that automates this workflow, completing in under 90 seconds in our internal testing. This approach reduces presentation creation time while grounding content in source documents. The solution deploys a supervisor agent on AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, using the Strands Agents framework to orchestrate document generation and summarization tools. Anthropic Claude Sonnet 4.6 (available on Amazon Bedrock) handles content creation, Amazon Titan Text Embeddings v2 powers vector search, and Stability AI Stable Image Inpaint (available on Amazon Bedrock) generates slide images. This post includes a public repository with the code assets.

 Solution overview

 The solution deploys a single supervisor agent on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime that selects between document generation and summarization tools based on user requests. A Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) pipeline uses Amazon OpenSearch Serverless for vector storage and semantic search across multimodal content.

 The solution includes a REST API built with .NET 8 minimal APIs, so you can integrate with existing enterprise applications through standard HTTP calls. AWS Lambda offers serverless compute, including containerized functions for PowerPoint generation. The solution secures the implementation with Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (Amazon VPC) isolation, AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) encryption, and AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) least-privilege access control.

 Key concepts

 This section covers AgentCore runtime, RAG, and content safety guardrails as they apply to this solution.

 Agent orchestration with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore

 A single AI agent generating documents from large knowledge bases must retrieve content, structure outlines, generate text, create images, and assemble files. Rather than implementing these competing responsibilities in a monolithic function, the solution uses a tool-based architecture where a supervisor agent routes requests to specialized tools.

 Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime provides a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with any framework or model. The agent code runs in an isolated container with session management, built-in identity, and observability. The solution uses the Strands Agents framework (an open source SDK for building AI agents) to implement the supervisor logic.

 The supervisor agent exposes two tools:

 generate_pptx: Creates PowerPoint presentations by invoking the PPTX Generator Lambda function, which retrieves content from the knowledge base, generates slide outlines, creates AI images, and assembles the final document.

 generate_summary: Extracts and synthesizes information from the knowledge base using RAG to deliver accurate, grounded responses.

 The agent determines whether a request requires document generation, content summarization, or both, then invokes the appropriate tool. You can add new capabilities by defining new tools in the agent code without modifying existing ones.

 Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) for enterprise knowledge

 RAG addresses a fundamental challenge in AI systems: delivering accurate, up-to-date information grounded in enterprise data rather than relying solely on the model’s training data. The implementation uses Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases , which combine vector search with large language models (LLMs) to retrieve relevant context before generating responses.

 The RAG pipeline works as follows:

 You upload enterprise documents to Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) .

 The system chunks and parses documents, applying special handling for multimodal content including tables, charts, and images.

 Amazon Titan Text Embeddings v2 converts each chunk into high-dimensional vectors that capture semantic meaning.

 Amazon OpenSearch Serverless stores the vectors, creating a searchable vector database.

 At query time, the system converts the user’s request into an embedding and performs similarity search to retrieve relevant document chunks.

 Retrieved chunks supply context to the language model, which generates responses grounded in the source material.

 This approach is designed to help reduce hallucinated content by grounding generated documents in source information from the enterprise knowledge base.

 Note: The Amazon OpenSearch Serverless collection data plane must remain publicly accessible because Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases accesses Amazon OpenSearch Serverless from AWS-managed infrastructure, not through customer VPC endpoints. IAM data access policies protect the collection, and VPC-only access restricts the Amazon OpenSearch Serverless dashboard.

 Amazon Bedrock Guardrails for content safety

 Enterprise AI applications require content moderation to meet organizational standards and compliance requirements. Amazon Bedrock Guardrails offers built-in content filtering and safety mechanisms integrated throughout the document generation pipeline.

 Guardrails operate at multiple stages:

 Input processing: Filters user requests to help prevent injection issues and inappropriate content.

 Output generation: Monitors model outputs to verify compliance with content policies.

 Personally identifiable information (PII) handling: Detects and anonymizes or blocks PII.

 The implementation creates custom guardrails through AWS Cloud Development Kit (AWS CDK) , configured with specific policies tailored to enterprise document creation. The agent applies guardrails at the model invocation level, providing consistent content safety without requiring manual configuration for each deployment.

 Solution architecture

 The following diagram illustrates the agent-based document generation system.

 Figure 1: Architecture of the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore RAG presentation generation system

 The data flow begins with user requests arriving through Amazon API Gateway , which routes them to a .NET-based Chat API running on AWS Lambda . The API maintains conversation state in Amazon DynamoDB . It then invokes the supervisor agent hosted on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime.

 The supervisor agent analyzes the request and selects the appropriate tool. For document generation, it invokes the PPTX Generator Lambda (a containerized Python function). For summarization, the supervisor invokes the Summary Generator Lambda, which queries the knowledge base through the retrieve_and_generate API.

 The system processes, chunks, and embeds documents stored in Amazon S3 using Amazon Titan Text Embeddings v2. Amazon OpenSearch Serverless indexes the embeddings for fast semantic search. When tools query the knowledge base, Amazon OpenSearch Serverless retrieves relevant chunks, which are then supplied as context to Anthropic Claude Sonnet 4.6 (on Amazon Bedrock) for generating grounded responses.

 The system stores generated documents in Amazon S3 and returns presigned URLs for secure download. Security measures include:

 AWS WAF with managed rule sets and IP-based rate limiting on Amazon API Gateway.

 Amazon Cognito with the Plus feature plan and advanced security mode for threat protection.

 Amazon Bedrock Guardrails provisioned through AWS CDK for consistent content filtering.

 Amazon DynamoDB with point-in-time recovery, deletion protection, and customer-managed AWS KMS encryption.

 Amazon S3 buckets with versioning, server access logging, and block public access.

 AWS X-Ray tracing on Lambda functions for distributed debugging.

 Input validation with regex-based tenant ID and session ID verification.

 Tenant isolation through AWS Security Token Service (AWS STS) role assumption per tenant.

 Prerequisites

 Before deploying, you need the following tools and access configured in your environment:

 AWS environment: 

 An active AWS account with permissions for deploying infrastructure.

 AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) configured with credentials.

 IAM role with appropriate service access policies.

 Development tools: 

 .NET SDK 8 with Amazon.Lambda.Tools installed globally.

 Python 3.12 or later for AWS CDK and Lambda functions.

 Node.js and AWS CDK CLI for infrastructure deployment.

 Docker or Finch for building container images (ARM64 support required).

 AWS services access: 

 Amazon Bedrock with model access for Anthropic Claude Sonnet 4.6, Amazon Titan Text Embeddings v2, and Stability AI Stable Image Inpaint (available through Amazon Bedrock). For model availability by Region, see Supported models by AWS Region in Amazon Bedrock .

 Amazon Bedrock AgentCore access enabled in your account.

 Amazon API Gateway Regional REST API integration timeout configured to at least 300 seconds. The default is 29 seconds. For more information, see API Gateway quotas .

 An existing Amazon VPC with private subnets.

 An Amazon S3 bucket for deployment artifacts.

 Set up the solution

 The setup process includes configuring deployment parameters and initializing the AWS CDK environment.

 Clone the repository and navigate to the project directory: 

 git clone https://github.com/aws-samples/sample-generating-powerpoint-presentations-with-amazon-bedrock.git 

 Create the configuration file pipeline-params.ini at the repository root: 

 environment=dev
awscliprofile=
ContainerRegistry=lambda-pptx-gen
AgentContainerRegistry=agentcore-supervisor
BucketDev=<amzn-s3-demo-bucket>
VpcId=<your-vpc-id>
ParsingInferenceProfileId=us.anthropic.claude-haiku-4-5-20251001-v1:0
AgentInferenceProfileId=us.anthropic.claude-sonne

items.title: How Tamnoon built AI-powered cloud security remediation with Amazon Bedrock
items.summary: Learn how Tamnoon built Tami, an agentic cloud remediation orchestrator on Amazon Bedrock that autonomously investigates and safely remediates cloud security findings from CNAPP and cloud-native sources. The approach drove a 90%+ reduction in critical cloud exposure in 90 days with zero production issues.
items.content:
Artificial Intelligence 

 How Tamnoon built AI-powered cloud security remediation with Amazon Bedrock

 Critical cloud exposures pile up faster than security teams can close them. Cloud-native application protection platforms (CNAPP), cloud providers, and posture scanners generate more findings than any team can triage, and risk accumulates in the gap between detected and fixed. Most findings sit untouched, not because they’re hard to fix. Someone must investigate context, identify the owner, confirm the fix won’t break production, and then do it at a volume that outpaces headcount.

 In this post, we share how Tamnoon built Tami, an agentic cloud remediation orchestrator on Amazon Bedrock , to close that gap. Tami autonomously investigates findings ingested from CNAPP and cloud-native sources and assesses whether remediation is safe. It then generates and orchestrates the fix with guardrails and governance wherever a change touches a customer’s cloud. The approach drove an over 90 percent reduction in critical cloud exposure in 90 days with zero production issues.

 About Tamnoon

 Tamnoon is an AI-powered cloud security remediation platform that works alongside CNAPPs. Its AI assistant, Tami, helps human cloud security experts investigate, prioritize, and safely remediate misconfigurations and issues across customer environments in AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, and other cloud providers.

 Tamnoon integrates with the CNAPPs and cloud-native tools teams already use and turns their findings into validated, production-safe fixes. Most of the work including investigation, prioritization, and remediation planning happens before anything touches a live environment, which is what makes automated remediation trustworthy at scale.

 Cloud security remediation challenges

 A security engineer can spend hours investigating a single finding. Often, it traces back to the same root cause as dozens of other alerts.

 Alert volume overwhelms headcount: CNAPPs and scanners generate thousands of findings. Teams can’t triage them all, so critical exposures sit unresolved while risk compounds for months.

 Investigation is manual and repetitive: Each finding requires context gathering on who owns the resource, what depends on it, whether the fix is safe. This eats hours of senior engineer time, repeated across every item in the backlog.

 Fear of production impact blocks automation: Teams hesitate to automate remediation because they can’t risk taking down production. Without confidence that a fix is safe, nothing moves.

 Reactive prioritization: Without a way to cluster related findings or score remediation confidence, teams work through alerts linearly rather than addressing root causes that resolve many issues at once.

 Tamnoon’s solution addresses the full pipeline from finding ingestion to validated fix. The platform treats these challenges as interconnected rather than isolated problems.

 Solution overview

 Tamnoon takes you from initial finding to executing the fix. The platform ingests findings from CNAPP, Cloud Security Posture Management (CSPM) providers, and other security tools and normalizes them into a unified schema. It then enriches them with asset and exposure context and prioritizes them. From there, the agentic layer takes over using a set of specialized AI agents, each running in an event-driven, serverless architecture on AWS, so every stage scales independently and fails safely.

 Agentic architecture on Amazon Bedrock

 The platform delegates work to four specialized agents, each responsible for a distinct phase of the remediation pipeline:

 An investigation agent draws on training from millions of real customer cloud environments to determine context, filters that context through a large language model (LLM)-as-a-judge validation layer. It reasons through the remediation goal, operational scope, and cloud-provider-specific verification, producing read-only investigation steps and a complete investigation plan.

 A safety-scoring agent builds an evidence chain per asset, combining automated verification results with analyst findings. It classifies each finding’s remediation as SAFE, RISKY, or AWAITING DATA with a deliberately conservative bias. When in doubt, it downgrades.

 A remediation agent activates only for findings that the safety agent has deemed safe. It reasons through ordering, dependencies, and conditions, then produces a remediation plan in which every step follows a backup, remediate, and verify structure and includes rollback guidance.

 A code-generation agent turns plan steps into executable remediation, but only after an input guardrail screens for relevance and prompt injection. Every artifact passes an automated generate-and-review loop in which a separate reviewer agent must approve the output.

 Why Amazon Bedrock

 When the Tamnoon team set out to build Tami, the choice of foundation model (FM) platform was going to shape everything that followed. Tamnoon’s remediation agents don’t all do the same kind of work. Some perform deep investigative reasoning to understand the root cause of a security finding. Others handle high-volume validation, checking proposed fixes quickly and cheaply. Still others review generated code, balancing quality against cost on every task. Matching each of these jobs to the right model, without stitching together a different integration for each one, was a core requirement.

 That requirement is what made Amazon Bedrock the natural fit. Through a single API, each agent can call the foundation model best suited to its task. The most capable models handle the hardest reasoning. More efficient models take on the repetitive, high-throughput work. Review-focused models optimize the trade-off between output quality and cost. Because it’s one integration rather than many, models can be swapped or upgraded as the landscape evolves, without re-plumbing the architecture each time.

 Operational overhead at scale was another factor in the decision. As request volume grew, Tamnoon wanted to avoid building and maintaining its own logic to distribute traffic across regional capacity. Amazon Bedrock Cross-Region inference handles this automatically. It automatically routes inference requests to the optimal AWS Region within a defined geographic boundary, maintaining throughput without requiring any custom routing code to operate.

 Security was the final consideration, and for a cloud security company it was non-negotiable. With Bedrock, inference runs inside Tamnoon’s own AWS environment under AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM)-scoped permissions. Sensitive customer data never leaves the trust boundary. That gave the team confidence that the platform underpinning Tami met the same standard Tamnoon holds its own service to.

 How Tamnoon integrates with CNAPPs and cloud security tools

 Tamnoon sits downstream of the detection tools security teams already run. CNAPPs like Wiz, CrowdStrike, Palo Alto Cortex, Upwind, SentinelOne, Orca, and Cyera along with cloud-native services like AWS Security Hub and Amazon GuardDuty are the source of truth for what’s wrong in the environment. Tamnoon connects through API-based integrations and normalizes findings into a common format, so a misconfiguration looks the same whether it came from Wiz or GuardDuty. The detection tools remain the foundation. Tamnoon delivers the end-to-end remediation that follows.

 For every finding it works, Tami assigns a Remediation Confidence Indicator (RCI) of SAFE, RISKY, or AWAITING DATA. That rating tells teams what can be automated and what needs human review first.

 Figure 1: Tamnoon in action

 Tamnoon AWS architecture

 Tamnoon runs entirely within its own AWS accounts, isolated per environment. Users access the platform through a single secure entry point built on Amazon API Gateway, with encryption managed by AWS Certificate Manager and sign-in handled by Amazon Cognito. Everything behind that entry point runs in private networks across multiple Availability Zones, so the core platform is never directly exposed to the internet.

 Inside that environment, Tamnoon combines two kinds of compute. Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) runs the always-on services behind the dashboard, while AWS Lambda powers the event-driven work of collecting findings, analyzing them, and executing remediations. A set of AWS messaging and workflow services, including Amazon EventBridge, Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS), and AWS Step Functions, coordinate these steps so large volumes of findings are processed reliably and in parallel, with no single bad record stalling the rest.

 The AI layer runs on Amazon Bedrock. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore , a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale with any framework or model, gives Tamnoon’s agents a governed way to take action instead of open-ended access. Amazon Bedrock Guardrails then review both the request and the generated code before anything moves forward. Supporting services handle the rest of the platform: managed databases and caching for state, Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) for playbooks and artifacts, and AWS Secrets Manager for credentials, so sensitive keys never live in application code.

 On the customer side, everything to the left of the AWS Cloud boundary is what customers connect into Tamnoon. They can link their own AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud accounts, plug in the security tools their findings come from, and connect the destinations where they want outcomes delivered, such as Slack, Jira, ServiceNow, and GitHub.

 How Tamnoon maintains zero production issues

 Zero production issues is a reality for Tamnoon’s customers, and it is no accident. Autonomy at Tamnoon sits inside a defense-in-depth safety architecture, where each layer assumes the one before it might miss something.

items.title: Deploy and evaluate models with Amazon SageMaker JumpStart
items.summary: Learn how to deploy an available model from Amazon SageMaker JumpStart, run a lightweight and repeatable performance test using the SageMaker Python SDK, and delete the endpoint when testing is complete.
items.content:
Artificial Intelligence 

 Deploy and evaluate models with Amazon SageMaker JumpStart

 Choosing the right model for a specific application requires a practical way to test it with representative inputs. Amazon SageMaker JumpStart provides access to a broad catalog of already pretrained models. In this post, we show how to deploy an available model from SageMaker JumpStart, run a lightweight and repeatable performance test using the SageMaker Python SDK, and delete the endpoint when testing is complete. For supported models and available capacity, this workflow provides a repeatable evaluation path, although deployment time varies by model, instance type, quota, and AWS Region.

 In 2026, SageMaker JumpStart introduced two improvements that simplify model discovery and deployment. In the Model Hub section of the Amazon SageMaker AI console, you can browse the SageMaker JumpStart catalog, view sample notebooks, and open them directly in SageMaker Studio. Pre-configured endpoint deployment options provide named configurations optimized for priorities such as low cost, low latency, or general-purpose workloads across a range of generative AI models, including Neuron-optimized configurations. Additionally, you can now go from Hugging Face model discovery to SageMaker AI deployment in a single click using the new deep link integration.

 Solution overview

 Our approach uses a reusable Python script that performs three steps:

 Discover and deploy a model from SageMaker JumpStart.

 Run model-specific sample prompts and measure latency, approximate output length, and single-request generation rate.

 Clean up the endpoint.

 This pattern works for many compatible SageMaker JumpStart models, although payload formats, required instance types, end-user license agreement (EULA) requirements, and response schemas may require model-specific adjustments.

 Prerequisites

 An AWS account with SageMaker AI permissions.

 Python 3+ with SageMaker Python SDK v3 installed ( pip install "sagemaker>=3,<4" ).

 Sufficient GPU instance quota for the model you want to test or request a quota increase .

 Step 1.a: Discover available models

 UI path to find models in SageMaker JumpStart:

 Figure 1: Browsing the model catalog on the SageMaker JumpStart Models page in SageMaker Studio

 Code path using SageMaker Python SDK:

 from sagemaker.core.jumpstart.notebook_utils import (
 list_jumpstart_models,
)

REGION = "us-east-1"

models = list_jumpstart_models(
 filter="task == textgeneration",
 region=REGION,
 list_versions=True,
)

print(f"Found {len(models)} text generation models")

for model_id, model_version in models[:10]:
 print(
 f" - {model_id} "
 f"(version {model_version})"
 ) 

 Or search by model name:

 from sagemaker.core.jumpstart.notebook_utils import list_jumpstart_models

ids = list_jumpstart_models(
 filter="model_id contains qwen",
 region=REGION,
 list_versions=True,
)

print(f"{len(ids)} models matched in {REGION}\n")

for model_id, version in ids:
 print(f"{model_id:<55} v{version}") 

 Step 1.b: Deploy the model

 UI path to deploy models from SageMaker JumpStart:

 Figure 2: Deploying a model from its SageMaker JumpStart detail page in SageMaker Studio

 Code path using SageMaker Python SDK:

 import time

from sagemaker.core.jumpstart.accessors import JumpStartModelsAccessor
from sagemaker.core.jumpstart.configs import JumpStartConfig
from sagemaker.core.training.configs import Compute
from sagemaker.serve import ModelBuilder

MODEL_ID = "huggingface-vlm-qwen3-5-27b"
MODEL_VERSION = "1.13.0"
REGION = "us-east-1"
ACCEPT_EULA = False # Set True only after reviewing the model terms

def get_field(value, name, default=None):
 if isinstance(value, dict):
 return value.get(name, default)
 return getattr(value, name, default)

# Resolve the JumpStart-recommended deployment configuration.
specs = JumpStartModelsAccessor().get_model_specs(
 region=REGION,
 model_id=MODEL_ID,
 version=MODEL_VERSION,
)

if isinstance(specs, list):
 if not specs:
 raise ValueError(
 f"No JumpStart specification found for {MODEL_ID}"
 )
 specs = specs[0]

recommended_instance_type = get_field(
 specs,
 "default_inference_instance_type",
)

if not recommended_instance_type:
 raise ValueError(
 f"No recommended instance type found for {MODEL_ID}"
 )

print(f"Model: {MODEL_ID}")
print(f"Region: {REGION}")
print(f"Recommended instance: {recommended_instance_type}")

start = time.time()

jumpstart_config = JumpStartConfig(
 model_id=MODEL_ID,
 model_version=MODEL_VERSION,
 accept_eula=ACCEPT_EULA,
)

model_builder = ModelBuilder.from_jumpstart_config(
 jumpstart_config=jumpstart_config,
 compute=Compute(
 instance_type=recommended_instance_type,
 instance_count=1,
 ),
)

model = model_builder.build()
endpoint = model_builder.deploy()
deploy_time = time.time() - start

print(f"Deployed in {deploy_time:.1f} seconds")
print(f"Endpoint: {endpoint.endpoint_name}") 

 Step 2: Run sample prompts and measure performance

 from sagemaker.core.payloads import retrieve_all_examples
import json
import time

MODEL_ID = "huggingface-vlm-qwen3-5-27b"
MODEL_VERSION = "1.13.0"
REGION = "us-east-1"

example_payloads = retrieve_all_examples(
 region=REGION,
 model_id=MODEL_ID,
 model_version=MODEL_VERSION,
 serialize=True,
)

#you can re-create the endpoint pointer using the endpoint name:
#from sagemaker.core.resources import Endpoint
#endpoint = Endpoint.get(endpoint_name="<your_endpoint_name>",region=REGION)

def read_response_body(result):
 body = result.body
 if hasattr(body, "read"):
 body = body.read()
 if isinstance(body, bytes):
 body = body.decode("utf-8")
 if isinstance(body, str):
 try:
 return json.loads(body)
 except json.JSONDecodeError:
 return body
 return body

def extract_output(response):
 """Handle common JumpStart text-generation response formats."""
 if isinstance(response, list):
 response = response[0] if response else ""
 if isinstance(response, dict):
 choices = response.get("choices")
 if choices:
 choice = choices[0]
 message = choice.get("message")
 if isinstance(message, dict):
 return message.get("content", "")
 return choice.get("text", "")
 for field in (
 "generated_text",
 "output_text",
 "text",
 ):
 if field in response:
 return response[field]
 return response

results = []

for payload in example_payloads or []:
 start = time.perf_counter()
 result = endpoint.invoke(
 body=payload.body,
 content_type=payload.content_type,
 accept=payload.accept,
 )
 latency = time.perf_counter() - start
 response = read_response_body(result)
 output = extract_output(response)
 if not isinstance(output, str):
 output = json.dumps(output, indent=2)
 # This is an estimate based on whitespace-separated words.
 output_words = len(output.split())
 results.append(
 {
 "request_preview": payload.body[:50],
 "latency_s": round(latency, 2),
 "estimated_output_words": output_words,
 "words_per_second": round(
 output_words / latency,
 1,
 ) if latency > 0 else 0,
 }
 )
 print("Input:\n", payload.body, end="\n\n")
 print("Output:\n", output, end="\n\n")
 print(
 f"Latency: {latency:.2f} seconds\n"
 f"Estimated output words: {output_words}\n"
 f"Estimated single-request output generation rate: "
 f"{output_words / latency:.1f} words/second\n"
 )
 print("-" * 80)

print("\nSummary:")
for result in results:
 print(result) 

 Result:

 Input:
{"max_tokens": 256, "messages": [{"content": "What is deep learning?", "role": "user"}], "model": "/opt/ml/model"}
Output:
Here's a thinking process that leads to the explanation of deep learning:
1. **Deconstruct the Request:**
* **Question:** "What is deep learning?"
* **Intent:** The user wants a clear, comprehensive, yet accessible definition and overview of deep learning.
* **Target Audience:** Likely someone looking for a general understanding, possibly a student, tech
enthusiast, or professional exploring the field. The tone should be informative, structured, and
not overly jargon-heavy (though key terms need explanation).
2. **Initial Brainstorming & Key Concepts:**
* What is it? A subset of machine learning, which is a subset of AI.
* Core mechanism: Artificial Neural Networks (ANNs).
* "Deep" means many layers (hidden layers).
* How does it work? Learning representations from data (feature learning).
* Key applications: Image recognition, NLP, speech, self-driving cars.
* Why is it popular now? Big data, GPU power, better algorithms.
* Pros/Cons: High accuracy vs. black box, data hunger.
3. **Structuring the Answer:**
Latency: 9.07 seconds
Estimated output words: 153
Estimated single-request output generation rate: 16.9 words/second
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Summary:
{'request_preview': '{"max_tokens": 256, "messages": {"content": "What', 'latency_s': 9.07, 'estimated_output_words': 153, 'words_per_second': 16.9} 

 Step 3: Cleanup

 print(f"Deleting endpoint: {endpoint.endpoint_name}")
endpoint.delete()
endpoint.wait_for_delete()
print("Endpoint deleted") 

 Conclusion

 This pattern works for many available SageMaker JumpStart models, but the payload format, required instance type, EULA, and response parsing may require model-specific adjustments. By using consistent test prompts and measuring latency, throughput, and output quality across models, you can compare options and select the right fit for your workload.

 Try this approach with different models from Amazon SageMaker JumpStart to find the right balance of quality, speed, and cost for your applications.

 References

 Benchmark and Optimize SageMaker JumpStart Deployment (blog post) 

 From Hugging Face to SageMaker Studio in One Click (blog post)

items.title: HiRO-ACEv2: Simulating extreme weather at 3 km resolution for a fraction of the cost
items.summary: HiRO-ACEv2 captures extreme rain, wind, and pressure events at 3 km resolution for about 1/300th the cost of X-SHiELD, making detailed global climate simulations more accessible to researchers.
items.content:
HiRO-ACEv2: Simulating extreme weather at 3 km resolution for a fraction of the cost
 October 14, 2026
 Ai2 

 Share 

 Models Tech Report Tutorial Notebooks Demo 

 We introduce HiRO-ACEv2 , the newest update to our High Resolution Output Ai2 Climate Emulator (HiRO-ACE) system. HiROv2 can reproduce even extremely rare rain, wind, and pressure events with high accuracy, while the full system can generate global 3 km climate data at about 1/300th the cost of X-SHiELD, a high-resolution global atmospheric model that explicitly simulates storms and other small-scale weather.
 HiRO-ACE, introduced earlier in 2026 , has two parts: ACE, an AI model that operates at a coarser 100 km resolution, and HiRO, a model that sharpens those coarse outputs into fine 3 km detail. The biggest change in HiRO-ACEv2 is the new downscaling model, HiROv2, which can now 1) predict several high-resolution fields at once instead of just rainfall, so it can capture a much wider range of extreme weather, and 2) has improved skill in predicting extreme events.
 Our main focus with HiRO-ACEv2 was to simulate extreme events well. Changes to how we train HiROv2 improved its ability to reproduce the most intense rain, wind, and pressure values. When given coarsened X-SHiELD data, it matches the target simulation's high-resolution statistics to within 3%, even for events so rare they occur only once in a million data points. It also accurately estimates the total energy of tropical cyclones, including storms it never saw during training, and generates hurricanes with realistic eyes and rain bands, though winds and pressure around the eye remain somewhat more lopsided than in X-SHiELD. Additionally, HiROv2 realistically generates strong winds flowing down mountain slopes.
 We also trained an updated version of ACE for this system. Over a 10-year simulation, its hurricanes, average climate patterns, and overall distributions of rain, wind, and pressure all line up well with X-SHiELD. That tells us ACE's coarse simulations are a solid foundation for producing long-term high-resolution climate data.
 Putting HiROv2 and ACE together, we generated a full year of global 3 km data. Its statistics closely match X-SHiELD's, even though HiRO was working from a simulation ACE ran on its own rather than from real X-SHiELD data. Across a 10-year run, the energy of HiRO-ACEv2's hurricanes is comparable to X-SHiELD's over the same period, and snapshots from that run show a variety of other extreme events that resemble those in X-SHiELD.

 An example of a strong hurricane in the North Atlantic, generated during the 10-year HiRO-ACEv2 simulation. 
 Overall, HiRO-ACEv2 offers researchers a flexible and inexpensive way to generate many versions of high-resolution rain, wind, and pressure data for extreme events over 10 years or more. Producing global high-resolution data with it costs roughly 300 times less than running X-SHiELD. If only one region is needed, the savings can be more than a hundred times greater, depending on the size of the area. We're also working on a streamlined version of HiROv2 that could make it more than ten times faster still.
 We still have future work ahead of us: because HiRO learned from X-SHiELD, it only works with the version of ACE tuned to match X-SHiELD. That means it can't yet produce high-resolution data for other climates, such as a warmer future or the historical record in datasets like ERA5. Next, we plan to train on new X-SHiELD datasets, including one simulating a world 4°C warmer, so the system can handle different climates. We also plan to add outputs like near-surface temperature and snow and ice, which would allow for even more uses, such as snowpack prediction.
 Visualizing and using HiRO outputs

 Simulated 10 m wind speed over Baja California in the ACE data visualizer: ACE2 at 100 km resolution on the main map and HiRO-ACEv2 at 3 km in the inset. 

 A simulated storm over the northeastern Pacific in the ACE data visualizer. The main map shows 10 m wind speed at 100 km resolution; the 3 km HiRO-ACEv2 inset shows finer structure within the storm. 
 To make it easy to see what HiRO produces without running any inference, we built a web demo that shows pre-generated precipitation, wind, and sea-level pressure output from HiROv1 and HiROv2 side by side with X-SHiELD, the simulation they were trained on. The demo complements the quantitative comparisons in our tech report : it offers a quick visual check of how the outputs look, and lets users zoom in on their own region of interest to judge performance there. 
 For more in-depth analysis, the models are available to download , and our tutorial notebooks walk through how to run them.

 “We’re committed to Singapore for the long term,” said Dale Finlay, General Manager of ASEAN at Anthropic. “Our customers here hold AI to an extremely high standard, especially when it comes to reliability and security. Having a team on the ground means we can get even closer to the organizations putting Claude to work on their hardest problems.”
 Supporting responsible AI in Singapore

 Kai Fong Chng, Permanent Secretary of the Ministry of Digital Development and Information, and Anthropic co-founder Ben Mann signed the MOU on the sidelines of Singapore International Cyber Week. Minister for Digital Development and Information Josephine Teo and Michael Sellitto, Anthropic Head of APAC Policy, witnessed the signing. It sets out areas of cooperation in AI safety, security, and model evaluation; research on AI adoption and its impact; and responsible adoption across the public and private sectors.

 “Singapore has been a leader in responsible AI, with a long track record of investment in model testing and evaluation,” said Mann. “We founded Anthropic on the belief that capability and safety have to go hand in hand. With this MOU, we’ll partner with Singapore to help ensure the transition to powerful AI goes well here, across Asia-Pacific, and around the world.”

 “Singapore’s approach to AI has always been to enable innovation while keeping pace with its evolving risks. Trust is critical for businesses, workers, and the public to use AI with confidence,” said Chng. “This partnership with Anthropic reflects the Government’s commitment to scaling up the responsible adoption of AI, deepening capabilities in our companies and government agencies, and delivering impact for Singapore.”

 Our work with Singapore goes back to 2023, when we joined the Generative AI Evaluation Sandbox run by the Infocomm Media Development Authority and the AI Verify Foundation. We later partnered with them on a red-teaming project in English, Mandarin, Malay, and Tamil.

 Under the MOU, we plan to hold technical exchanges with Singapore’s AI safety, security, and assurance institutions on model evaluation, testing standards, and incident response. We do similar work with safety institutes around the world, where sharing technical information provides governments with a clearer view of frontier AI capabilities and risks, while helping developers build safer models.

 We’ll also look for ways to strengthen AI skills in Singapore, help small and medium-sized businesses adopt AI responsibly, and support the government’s goal of building AI capability among public officers. We plan to share research and data with the government, including from the Anthropic Economic Index , and to offer technical and policy expertise as Singapore develops its rules for AI.
 How Singapore is working with Claude

 In our latest Economic Index , Singapore ranks second of 121 countries in Claude.ai usage relative to its population, at nearly six times what its size alone would predict.

 In the public sector, more than 1,500 engineers and technical staff at the Government Technology Agency of Singapore (GovTech Singapore) have adopted Claude Code to modernize government systems and speed up software delivery. This has helped GovTech Singapore teams build, maintain, and enhance digital services more efficiently at national scale. The Cyber Security Agency of Singapore is exploring how Claude could help strengthen the country’s cyber defense.

 In financial services, DBS, Southeast Asia’s largest bank, works with Claude across a range of use cases in its Singapore operations—including software development and day-to-day productivity—as part of its broader AI innovation efforts. These applications operate within the bank’s strict security and governance framework. GIC, Singapore’s sovereign wealth fund, is rolling out Claude across its investment and corporate services teams. Organizations in regulated sectors like financial services can now run Claude with in-region inference on Amazon Bedrock, helping them meet strict data processing requirements.

 Singapore’s largest technology companies and startups are building with Claude too. Grab powers BriX, its sales assistant, with Claude. The assistant saves Grab’s sales teams approximately 40,000 hours every quarter and surfaces new sales opportunities. Sea—the business behind Shopee, Garena, and Monee—works with Claude to help Shopee’s customer service chatbot respond faster and more accurately, and thousands of its employees write and debug code with Claude. And Supabase—the developer platform with strong roots in Singapore—is building with Claude Code.
 Building with the developer community

 This week, senior leaders from Anthropic are in Singapore to open the office and meet with customers, developers, and policymakers.

 Today, we hosted Builder Summit Singapore, bringing more than 300 developers together with engineering and product leaders from Anthropic. Earlier in the week, Singapore’s Claude community ambassadors held a meetup for more than 700 local builders.

 Discrete diffusion models have emerged as strong alternatives to autoregressive language models, with recent work initializing and finetuning a base unimodal model for bi-modal generation. Diverging from previous approaches, we introduce the first tri-modal Masked Diffusion Models (MDM) pretrained from scratch on text, image-text, and audio-text data. We systematically analyze multimodal scaling laws, modality mixing ratios, noise schedules, batch-size effects and provide optimized inference sampling defaults. Our batch-size analysis yields a novel stochastic differential equation (SDE) based reparameterization, eliminating the need for tuning the optimal batch size as reported in recent work. This reparameterization decouples the physical batch size, often chosen based on compute (GPU saturation, FLOP-efficiency, wall-clock time) from the logical batch size, chosen to balance the variance of gradients during stochastic optimization. Finally, we pretrain a preliminary model showcasing the capabilities of a unified design, achieving strong results at 3B model scale (6.4T tokens), in both text generation, T2I tasks, and T2S tasks. Our work represents the largest scale systematic open study of multimodal discrete diffusion models conducted to date, providing valuable insights into scaling behaviors across multiple modalities.

 Code-Switching Detection via Language-Selective Dimensions in Speech Foundation Models

 Authors Jie Chi, Zakaria Aldeneh, Masha Fedzechkina, Maureen de Seyssel, Natalie Schluter

 View publication 
 Copy Bibtex 

 Code-switching (CS), the alternation between languages within an utterance, is common in multilingual speech but underrepresented in pretraining corpora. Increasing CS coverage requires finding relevant utterances in large speech collections so that they can be included in training data. One way to find such utterances is to transcribe the speech and detect language alternation in the text, but this depends on obtaining accurate multilingual transcriptions. We propose a lightweight method that detects CS directly from speech. It uses frame-level language information in pretrained speech encoders to determine whether both languages are present within an utterance. Specifically, we identify language-selective hidden-state dimensions using monolingual recordings and aggregate their frame-level activations into a CS prediction. With a small CS set used to tune a decision rule, we show that the Whisper-small encoder achieves a mean F1 of 0.798 across 14 language pairs in CS-FLEURS, compared with 0.776 for a CNN and 0.751 for a HuBERT linear baseline trained for monolingual language identification. Our findings suggest that pretrained speech encoders already encode the information needed to identify CS utterances, and they provide a lightweight tool for building more representative multilingual corpora.

items.title: lessons from scaling teams of frontier coding agents
items.content:
Oct 14, 2026

 17 minute read

 Lessons from scaling teams of coding agents: reach the frontier at 30% of the cost
 Teams of coding agents are already building large-scale software, but how should they be organized to work most effectively and efficiently?

 Blog Written By
 Keenan Samway

 Daniel D'souza
 Research Engineer

 Nouha Dziri
 Senior Research Scientist

 Tags
 Research 
 Open Science 

 Share

 AI isn’t a shortcut. 
It’s how business gets ahead.
 Contact sales 
 Key takeaways
 Teams of agents unlock a new axis of inference-time scaling. On challenging coding tasks, well-organized teams outperform single agents, with gains of up to ~10 percentage points on ProgramBench. But these gains come at 3–7× higher cost. The question is not whether more agents help, but how to make that additional compute count.
 Where you allocate agents matters more than how many you add. On ProgramBench, delegating only exploration and planning matches the performance of delegating planning, implementation, and verification together at half the cost. Collaboration pays off most when agents target the task's actual bottleneck.
 A strong lead with cheap workers delivers near-frontier performance at 70% lower cost. A Sol lead coordinating 16 inexpensive Luna planning workers reaches 61.8% reward, compared with 63.2% for an all-Sol team delegating every stage, while reducing cost from $510 to $155.

 Agent teams are building software
 In the past year, teams of coding agents have moved from interesting demos to building large-scale software projects. Sixteen Claude agents wrote a 100,000-line C compiler that can build the Linux kernel, in a project that took about 2,000 agent sessions and $20,000 in API costs [ 1 ]. Cursor ran hundreds of agents that together wrote a web browser from scratch, more than a million lines of code, in about a week [ 2 ]. Bun was ported from Zig to Rust in 11 days, with 64 Claude agents running in parallel at its peak [ 3 ].
 Each of these teams produced working software, but they differ from one another in many ways at once, from the models and roles to the scope of the projects themselves. The C compiler's agents worked as peers with no orchestrator and claimed tasks through lock files. Cursor used a hierarchical structure, with planners recursively decomposing work into subtasks delegated to hundreds of worker agents. Bun assigned fixed roles, giving each piece of work to one implementer, two adversarial reviewers, and one fixer.
 Comparing them, however, says little about which design choices mattered or what they cost compared to a single agent. Factory's study of their own multi-agent system, which cycles an orchestrator, an implementer, and a validator in a fixed loop, shows how large that cost can be [ 4 ]. On one task, rebuilding the geospatial library GDAL, their three-role team more than doubled the reward achieved by a single agent, nearly reaching behavioral parity with the reference program, but cost 14 times as much and took 13 times as long.
 So agent teams can do more than a single agent, but they cost more to run and usually take longer. This raises an important question: if a team of agents is a new way to spend inference compute, how should it be organized to be both effective and efficient? To answer it, we built a controlled testbed and ran teams of coding agents on it.

 Figure 1. An illustrative run of a coding-agent team. A lead hands out work to its workers, who explore the original program, write code, and check it in a shared workspace.
 A controlled testbed
 A minimal harness 
 We built a deliberately minimal harness, inspired by mini-SWE-agent [ 5 ], so that we could change one design choice at a time. Every agent works through a simple bash tool, in one workspace shared by the whole team. One agent, the lead, receives the task and hands out work with a delegate_agent tool. A worker sees only the subtask it is given and reports back when it is done. Given the task, the lead dynamically decides how many workers to spawn, what each one does, and how to consolidate what they return. 1 
 Each delegate_agent call either starts a new worker with a fresh context window or resumes a worker the lead has used before. A resumed worker keeps its prior context, so the lead can follow up with an agent that already knows part of the program. For example, the lead can ask a worker to fix the bugs in the code it wrote, instead of briefing a new worker from scratch.
 From there, we vary five things:
 Where the lead uses workers. We instruct the lead agent with two main prompts, which differ in how much guidance they give. The minimal prompt tells the lead that it is in charge of a team and asks it to give workers distinct, independent tasks, but leaves everything else, from how many workers to use to how to decompose the task, to the lead. The PIV prompt adds a structured workflow of exploring and planning (P), implementing (I), and verifying (V), and asks the lead to use workers in all three stages.
 How the lead waits. A blocking lead waits for its workers to report back and does nothing in the meantime. An asynchronous lead keeps working while they run, and has two more tools, wait_for_updates to wait for the next report and list_agents to check on its workers.
 Which models play which role. Does every agent on the team need the strongest, most expensive model? We test this with two kinds of teams. In a homogeneous team, the lead and its workers all run the same model. In a heterogeneous team, the lead keeps the strong model, but the workers run a cheaper one. Think of a senior engineer who directs the work and makes critical decisions, with junior engineers doing most of the legwork.
 How many workers there are. Is a bigger team always better? To explore this, we compare two setups. In the first, the lead decides on its own how many workers it needs. In the second, we fix the team size at two, four, eight, or sixteen workers and see how reward and cost change as the team grows.
 How agents communicate. By default, all communication goes through the lead, which hands out each subtask and receives each worker's report. In one set of runs, we provide agents with a send_message tool and let them message each other directly.

 Figure 2. Two leads hand out the same subtasks, and each worker run takes the same time. The blocking lead sits idle until its workers report back. The asynchronous lead keeps working and starts the second round as soon as the first reports arrive. Bars are spans of work, downward arrows are calls to delegate_agent , and upward arrows carry reports back to the lead. Timings are illustrative.
 ProgramBench
 We test these choices on ProgramBench [ 6 ], a benchmark of 200 programs to rebuild from scratch. In each task, the agent starts from an empty workspace with the original program's executable, which it can run but not read, and that program's documentation. It has to probe the program to discover its interface, edge cases, and behavior, then write a new implementation that behaves the same way. We score each task by the share of a hidden suite of behavioral tests that the rebuilt program passes, and average this score over tasks to get the reward we report throughout. 2 
 The tasks range from small command-line utilities like jq and ripgrep to large systems like SQLite, FFmpeg, and the PHP interpreter. The most challenging remain far out of reach. On FFmpeg, the best entry on the public leaderboard passes about 10% of tests.
 Each task needs all three stages of the workflow, figuring out what the program does, writing it, and checking it against the original. That makes ProgramBench a good testbed for seeing which stages benefit from extra agents.

 Figure 3. One ProgramBench task, dsq , a command-line tool that runs SQL queries over JSON, CSV, and other data files. The top panel is a solo Sol agent with the minimal prompt, and the bottom panel an asynchronous Sol team with the PIV prompt. The solo agent writes its program as one Python file, while the team splits it into modules, some written by workers. The team panel follows the files of one run, commands are simplified from the agents' own, and timings are illustrative.

 We focus primarily on three GPT-5.6 models, Luna, Terra, and Sol, in increasing order of capability and cost. Unless noted otherwise, we ran each configuration three times on all 200 ProgramBench tasks and report averages over the three runs for reward, total cost, and total wall-clock time. A single task's score varied from run to run with a standard deviation of about 6 points, but the benchmark-wide average was far steadier, with a standard deviation of 0.5 points for a typical configuration and 1.4 for the noisiest. Every configuration ran on the same tasks, so we compare each team with its solo baseline task by task and report 95% confidence intervals of those differences.
 We also ran Commit0-Lite [ 7 ], a set of 16 Python libraries whose implementations have been removed. The agent is given each library's repository skeleton, documentation, and unit tests, and has to fill in the code so that the tests pass. In ProgramBench, the agent has to work out what to build by running the original program. In Commit0, these provided materials spell it out, so the benchmark shows whether the same stages pay off when the specification is already given. With only 16 tasks, we use it as a secondary check.
 Teams outperform solo agents, at a cost
 We start with the simplest comparison, a single Sol agent against a team of Sol agents. With the same minimal prompt, a blocking team passed 61.8% of tests on average, against 52.1% for the solo agent. Giving the solo agent the PIV prompt closed part of that gap (57.7%), but a blocking team with the PIV prompt still came out about 5 points ahead (63.1%).

 We also ran both prompts with an asynchronous lead, which can keep working while its workers run. All four Sol teams cost between 4 and 7 times as much a

Putting Earth AI to work: Geospatial agents for our planet's biggest challenges

 October 14, 2026
 Shravya Shetty, Distinguished Engineer, and Luke Barrington, Product Director, Google Research

 In a new technical report, we demonstrate how combining domain-specific foundation models, spatial tools, and upfront planning enables a Geospatial Reasoning agent to carry out complex spatial analysis and planetary prediction that standalone LLMs can’t. Following promising tests with partners, we’re also expanding experimental agent access via Ask Google Earth and an Agent-to-Agent (A2A) service.

 Quick links

 Microsite 

 Technical report 

 Interest form 

 Research@ top 10

 Share
