 ×

 When we introduced Google Earth AI , we shared a suite of geospatial foundation models — spanning remote sensing, weather, flood hydrology, and population dynamics — alongside an initial prototype showing how a Gemini-powered agent could connect those models to answer cross-modal questions.
 Since then, we have evolved a Geospatial Reasoning agent from an early concept into a much more capable, experimental system built for multi-step, geospatial reasoning across planet-scale data and autonomous training of custom predictive models. Today, we are sharing three updates:
 A new technical report on geospatial reasoning: We present systematic evaluations across four benchmarks, including GeoKTools and GeoExpertQueries, two new benchmarks we developed and are releasing for researchers to test their own geospatial reasoning agents. Our results quantify the value of Earth AI’s specialized tools and planning over out-of-the-box LLMs.
 Insights from real-world partner testing: Over the past few months, we invited a small group of social impact and commercial partner organizations — including the World Health Organization (WHO) Regional Office for Africa , People in Need , GiveDirectly , the Milken Institute and WPP — to test the agent in support of their own real-world workflows, such as disease outbreak investigations, disaster preparedness, and clean energy screening.
 Expanding early access on Google Earth and Google Cloud: We are expanding experimental access for both multi-step geospatial analysis and for planetary prediction. We’re offering early access to an experimental deep research update for Ask Google Earth . We’re also providing early access to an agent-to-agent API for developers building custom workflows, including integration recipes for connecting to Gemini .

 What’s new in Geospatial Reasoning

 General-purpose LLMs and standard coding tools struggle with real-world spatial problems because planetary datasets are massive, with specialized map and satellite formats that require careful multi-step planning to combine accurately. To tackle complex spatial workflows in practice, our agent brings together four key capabilities:

 Connected to Earth AI foundation models and planet-scale data

 The agent connects Gemini to the capabilities of Earth AI’s foundation models — including WeatherNext , Flood Forecasting , the Population Dynamics Foundation Model (PDFM) , AlphaEarth Foundations and Remote Sensing Foundations — alongside information from Google Maps Platform (e.g., place information, routing, air quality, rooftop solar potential), Google Earth Engine , Data Commons and Google Dataset Search .

 Modular skills, upfront planning and a dedicated spatial workspace

 Earth AI capabilities are packaged as modular skills that the agent calls only when a user question needs them. Before running complex operations, the agent builds a step-by-step analytical plan, selects appropriate fallback datasets when local coverage is sparse, and processes large map layers in a dedicated workspace. This approach avoids overwhelming the agent context with massive amounts of spatial data, while preserving accuracy and tracking data attribution. Every response shows the agent’s plan and the data sources used so experts can check assumptions or substitute datasets.

 Bring your own data

 Organizations rarely rely on public data alone. Users can now input their own datasets via the Geospatial Reasoning agent API as CSV spreadsheets, custom map boundaries ( GeoJSON ), or cloud tables. Users can then ask the agent to join their private locations with Earth AI’s global models and catalogs.

 From multi-step reasoning to autonomous Planetary Prediction

 Beyond answering complex analytical questions, the agent also powers our recently announced Planetary Prediction Engine . Given a user’s local outcome data, such as regional disease rates, crop yields, or grid outages, the agent automatically selects relevant population and environmental signals, fuses our Population Dynamics Insights and Custom Satellite Embeddings (Google Maps Platform products built on PDFM and AlphaEarth Foundations, respectively) and trains validated machine learning models for spatial prediction, super-resolution downscaling, and forecasting. In our recent public health research , combining these population and satellite signals improved predictions of health outcomes by 12% over demographic baselines and enabled mapping at 8X finer spatial resolution.

 Our Geospatial Reasoning agent responds to a user’s question by first planning a multistep workflow, then selecting key Earth AI tools, datasets and models that are relevant to the query, and finally executing each stage of the plan in a workspace outside the context window. The answer incorporates multiple Earth AI capabilities into a text, tabular and map-based report. 

 Evaluating a Geospatial Reasoning agent

 To measure the impact of domain-specific tools and upfront planning on geospatial reasoning, our technical report compares four agent configurations across Gemini 3.8 Flash and Gemini 3.1 Pro: (1) a standalone LLM, (2) the LLM with basic web search and maps grounding tools, (3) the LLM with Earth AI tools (such as Remote Sensing Foundations and WeatherNext 3) but without upfront planning, and (4) the full Geospatial Reasoning agent which begins every query with a dedicated planning stage that reasons over available capabilities to assess what it can and cannot do and sets out the stages of retrieval and processing needed to reach an answer.

 We evaluate four agent configurations, from the base Gemini model, to agents progressively augmented with skills and orchestration that are optimized for geospatial reasoning. 

 The evaluation spans four benchmarks, covering expert-level open-ended analysis, multi-tool orchestration, and community-developed geospatial problems with deterministic answers. CBGB and UnivEARTH are two externally developed benchmarks that test geospatial code generation and question answering respectively. To test agents on challenging tasks that go beyond a single question or use case, we developed two new benchmarks. GeoExpertQueries introduces complex, real-world queries with expert-authored golden workflows that capture analysis best practices in domains like crisis resilience, site selection and public health. GeoKTools contains templated queries with verifiable answers, each requiring correct selection and use of 1 to 4 distinct geospatial tools. Together, this suite provides substantially broader coverage than prior evaluations of geospatial reasoning systems. To accelerate research and development of geospatial agents, we release the development splits of both our new benchmarks in full.

 Example queries from our new GeoKTools ( left ) and GeoExpertQueries ( right ) benchmarks. GeoKTools tests an agent’s ability to select and use specific geospatial tools and datasets while GeoExpertQueries evaluates reasoning on open-ended, multi-step workflows. 

 Results and key takeaways

 Two key takeaways stand out from our evaluation: First, domain-specific skills are essential for spatial reasoning. The agent with only basic tools (web search, maps grounding and code execution) struggles on quantitative spatial tasks. Equipping the agent with Earth AI skills drives a significant jump across GeoExpertQueries, GeoKTools, and CBGB. The only exception is UnivEARTH, where even a standalone LLM scores 93.6%, likely because the source NASA articles and answers are available on the public web.
 Second, upfront planning unlocks open-ended, real-world workflows. While Earth AI skills alone are enough for narrower tasks like those in CBGB and GeoKTools, tackling open-ended problems in GeoExpertQueries requires upfront planning to keep the agent on track across multi-step analyses and prevent it from making unreliable assumptions or taking shortcuts like using web-search instead of spatial tools.

 Scores are 0–100, averaged over three runs. Each benchmark is scored differently, so compare within a row, not across rows. 

 The technical report also discusses limitations. GeoExpertQueries scores come from an autorater that compares the agent’s performance to expert workflows that define the steps an analysis should take, not the correct final answer. We therefore consider the agent’s output as a strong first draft for experts to review and build on, not a final answer.

 Earth AI in action: Early testing with partners

 To evaluate how this research translates to real-world challenges, we gave a small group of partners early access to test the experimental agent on their toughest problems. items.content:
Analyzing technical documents with Deep Review

 October 14, 2026
 Rajesh Jayaram and Vincent Cohen-Addad, Research Scientists, Google Research

 Following successful deployments across 16,000+ submissions at STOC, ICML, NeurIPS, and ICLR, Deep Review is launching publicly. It’s expanding from deep mathematical and scientific peer review to provide rigorous, grounded verification across knowledge documents, including Google Docs and presentations.

 Quick links

 Paper 

 STOC 2026 Blog Post 

 ICML 2026 Retrospective 

 NeurIPS 2026 Blog Post 

 Google Labs Portal 

 R@ Top 10 Blog 

 News from Google R@ Collection Page 

 Share 

 Copy link 

 ×

 Generative AI has accelerated many technical fields. It is now common for AI to play some role in writing scientific papers and technical documents, running code, designing experiments, and drafting proposals. However, accelerating content creation has created a review challenge: the human capacity for verification has remained largely fixed amid this rapid increase in AI-generated content. Reviewing complex documents like long scientific manuscripts or complex legal agreements requires specialized expertise and advanced subject knowledge. This imbalance creates a validation bottleneck , where information is being generated faster than it can be rigorously reviewed.
 Today, we’re excited to announce the public release of Deep Review , an agentic AI system engineered to provide rigorous feedback and technical verification on complex documents. Initially designed for computer science academic paper analysis, the system’s capabilities have expanded to review documents across many domains, such as legal and finance. It can be used as both an iterative improvement tool during the drafting process and a tool for the scientific process verification, claims, and evaluation during the review process.
 Deep Review represents the evolution of our Paper Assistant Tool (PAT) — an experimental initiative developed to help researchers stress-test manuscripts prior to conference submission. Over the past year, we partnered with four flagship computer science conferences ( STOC 2026 , ICML 2026, NeurIPS 2026, and ICLR 2027 ) to provide private, pre-submission feedback to authors of more than 16,000 manuscripts who opted in. Further details on PAT and these pilots can be found in our manuscript, Towards Automating Scientific Review with Google’s Paper Assistant Tool .
 With this release, Deep Review is now accessible worldwide:
 Tiered access and scalable API : Every user receives two complimentary document reviews per day. Users with high-volume workflows can connect their Gemini API key for higher usage limits and programmatic integration via the Deep Review API.
 Format flexibility : Deep Review will initially support PDFs and plain text as input formats, with support for multi-file inputs coming soon.
 Privacy and data policy : Documents uploaded to Deep Review are never used to train, fine-tune, or improve Google models. Uploaded documents are stored for one year for the sole purpose of display to the user in the Deep Review UI.

 Deep Review accelerates technical validation

 One of the most significant examples of the validation bottleneck is in academic peer review. This can be seen in the uptick of submissions to academic publication venues, especially venues for AI research itself, which have seen a dramatic rise. This year, there were over 74,000 submissions to three major AI conferences ( ICLR , NeurIPS , and ICML ) up from approximately 45,000 in 2025, 32,000 in 2024, and 23,000 in 2023. Each of these submissions requires multiple high-quality reviews to ensure the integrity of the peer review process, which can place a larger burden on human experts.

 Increase in submissions to NeurIPS, ICML, and ICLR between 2023 and 2026. 

 Deep Review aims to help alleviate this expanding burden on human reviewers across technical fields. By providing detailed, objective evaluations of documents, Deep Review checks logical consistency and mathematical statements, suggests improvements, grounds facts, and compares with existing work. It addresses some of the most cognitively burdensome facets of review, while leaving higher-level judgements to humans.

 A proven track record for scientific review

 Deep Review has been extensively tested and deployed under its experimental name, the Paper Assistant Tool (PAT), in four pilot partnerships with the flagship computer science conferences STOC 2026, ICML 2026, NeurIPS 2026, and ICLR 2027. During these pilots, authors were able to opt-in to receive feedback and analysis on their paper via PAT in the weeks before the submission deadline. The goal was to provide authors with actionable feedback to help improve the quality of papers in submission. This feedback was completely decoupled from the official conference review process. PAT did not collect any of the data for training, and papers were deleted from Google systems promptly after each program concluded.
 Author reactions to the tool have been extremely positive, and reflect continued improvements to both underlying models and the PAT harness. With the addition of Gemini 4 Argon support in Deep Review, the underlying capabilities of the tool have further increased beyond the older iterations of PAT described below.

 Statistics and author feedback from the pilot programs of PAT at machine learning and theoretical computer science conferences. 

 How Deep Review works

 Single-prompt LLM calls often fail when evaluating long, complex documents due to exhausting their token reasoning budget, overlooking long-context cross-section dependencies, or accepting nuanced claims without fully scrutinizing them. Deep Review solves these challenges through a four-stage agentic pipeline:
 Document segmentation : The document is first ingested and autonomously decomposed by a segmenter agent into logical segments (e.g., Introduction, experiments, methodology, etc.). These segments can be overlapping, and must cover all the content of the input document.
 Adaptive budgeting : Not all sections require equal cognitive depth. The pipeline inspects information density and dynamically allocates a compute budget, along with a specialized inference scaling pipeline for each section. For instance, sections with dense mathematical proofs may receive more compute than an introduction or a related work section in an academic paper.
 Deep parallel verification : Specialized reasoning agents scrutinize each segment in parallel. Each agent has access to the full document context to track cross-references, but focuses its reasoning power specifically on the task of reviewing its specific target section. This ensures both that reviewing tasks are manageable for each review swarm, and that parallel swarms are properly coordinated.
 Global synthesis and agentic grounding : A dedicated synthesis agent consolidates the segment-level reports, and does final consistency checks between sections, rerunning logical checks if required. The agent further performs external grounding checks and tool calls as a final preventative measure against hallucinations.

 System architecture showing the four-stage pipeline. 

 Universal verification and review: Beyond research papers

 While Deep Review originated in academic paper reviews, long-context review is generalizable: reasoning mechanisms used to check whether a mathematical proof holds up in a research paper can also help surface logical gaps and inconsistencies in other types of documents, where claims must be backed by evidence. Therefore, Deep Review can be used to bring structured critique to a broader range of everyday workflows.
 Users can now apply Deep Review to analyze complex documents across many domains. For instance, it can be run on:
 Design documents: Catch unstated architectural assumptions, spot edge cases, and suggest concrete improvements.
 Presentations: Ensure slide transitions flow logically and bulleted takeaways match visual charts.
 Legal and financial documents: Check internal consistency across clauses and data tables, flag ambiguous terms or downstream consequences, and ground claims against supporting evidence.

 Deep Review meets Antigravity

 We’re also introducing the Teamwork Deep Document Review Pattern , a document review implementation pattern inspired by Deep Review built into Antigravity using the Teamwork multi-agent orchestration framework . This pattern is designed systematically to evaluate research papers, manuscript drafts, and technical proposals using a multi-agent hierarchy with self-correction and segment-based rubrics. Antigravity users can invoke this pattern using the /teamwork-preview command.

 Making thorough, high-quality technical reviews widely accessible

 Comprehensive pre-submission critique in computer science has generally depended on access to extensive review networks — like senior faculty, well-resourced academic laboratories, or extensive peer advisory networks. Providing reliable, automated logical verification can help many academics stress-test their assertions, identify avoidable flaws, refine and strengthen their documents based on verified foundations, and present their work in a review process with more confidence.

 Get started

 We invite researchers, engineers, and creators everywhere to explore Deep Review:
 Try Deep Review: Visit the Google Research Portal to review your first documents.
 Integrate with the API: Access programmatic verification in your continuous integration and drafting workflows using your Gemini API key .
 Read the research: Read the preprint to explore the underlying methodology and pilot evaluations.

 Conclusion and looking ahead

 Given the utility it demonstrated during our pilot programs with academic conferences, we believe that tools like Deep Review will play a significant role across the peer review process in the coming years by empowering both authors and reviewers.

 Today, at our flagship Research@ event, we're sharing research breakthroughs that amplify human ingenuity. From planetary intelligence to advanced medical workflows, we’re putting capabilities once out of reach in the hands of people worldwide. Here are 10 highlights.

 We are living through a golden age of research and scientific discovery. For the scientists and researchers at Google Research, the opportunity extends beyond pioneering breakthroughs. We’re also building and sharing robust tools that empower the global ecosystem. AI acts as an amplifier of human ingenuity, creating the conditions for curiosity and rigorous inquiry to flourish.
 Today, at our Research@ event in Mountain View, we are demonstrating how we put never-before-possible insights and capabilities into the hands of doctors, scientists, developers, public health officials, and others.
 Here are 10 highlights:

 1. Google Earth AI enables planetary intelligence for organizations and society

 Addressing global challenges requires accurate, real-world planetary intelligence. With Google Earth AI , it becomes possible to forecast public health threats , accelerate clean energy investments, provide businesses with foresight, and more. Today, we’re expanding early access and inviting partners to explore three new ways to access Google Earth AI’s new, experimental capabilities :
 Conducting deeper geospatial analysis as part of an early access experimental feature in Google Earth .
 Generating risk assessments and forecasting different scenarios via our planetary prediction engine .
 Integrating our Geospatial Reasoning agent skills directly into custom workflows via an experimental agent-to-agent API, provides developers with programmatic access to core features like satellite imagery parsing, routing and demographic embeddings.
 We’re also announcing the integration of Google Dataset Search for querying from more than 100 million public datasets, and TimesFM for planetary nowcasting and forecasting iterations. All these capabilities are powered by over 70 geospatial tools including planetary foundation models like Remote Sensing Foundation Model (RSFM) and Population Dynamics Foundation Model (PDFM). They are validated by empirical benchmarks detailed in today’s Earth AI Technical Report . They enable developers, health leaders and enterprise teams to automate complex geospatial workflows.
 To further support social impact efforts, Google.org is providing $10 million in funding to organizations working on crisis resilience and public health. This includes $2 million to The Milken Institute to unlock infrastructure bottlenecks for affordable housing, clean energy, broadband, safe water systems, and other essential infrastructure.

 Google Earth AI ’s geospatial foundation models are being used to help predict disease outbreaks and enable public health teams to take proactive, preventive action. 

 2. Multi-agent orchestration helps scientists build on existing knowledge

 Existing literature offers a great source of knowledge for driving new scientific discoveries. We built a multi-agent orchestrator, enabling scientists to reproduce previous methods and analyses and then apply them in new settings to tackle important research challenges. As an example, this helped researchers apply a new methodology for solving inverse design problems in fluid mechanics to the design of urinary catheters. They discovered catheter designs that, in simulation, were better at preventing bacterial infections.
 This complements our existing tools to accelerate scientific workflows. Empirical Research Assistance enables scientists to generate and test thousands of code variations in parallel, and has helped researchers produce results from biology to cosmology to economics. Co-Scientist , built in collaboration with Google DeepMind, is a multi-agent tool that can generate novel hypotheses and has already helped partners, like researchers at Stanford University, uncover repurposed medicines to fight liver fibrosis.

 3. Deep Review helps authors improve the clarity and accuracy of technical documents

 Thorough peer review is a core part of the scientific method. We created Deep Review , an agentic system that provides rigorous verification across complex documents. This is particularly important as AI is increasingly being used to help experts draft technical documents. Many Google researchers and external authors have already used an early version of this system to review over 16,000 research publications submitted to top-tier computer science conferences. It helps with the heavy cognitive lifting by checking logical consistency and grounding facts, while scientists maintain authority over creative direction. Today, we’re expanding access to Deep Review to the general public to help people verify a variety of technical documents from legal agreements to financial reports.

 System architecture showing the four-stage pipeline. 

 4. Next-gen Edge AI chip enables manufacturers to build the wearables of tomorrow

 With the rise of wearable devices, hardware manufacturers need the tools to develop efficient edge applications to meet the high expectations of customers for all-day performance. Earlier this year, we launched the first Coralboard from Synaptics , using Google’s Coral NPU accelerator core. It enables AI and ML engineers to rapidly prototype and build devices. Next week, we’ll be revealing our co-designed, next-gen, low-power Edge AI chip, created by Synaptics using our open source IP. The chip delivers greater efficiency and performance for design engineers building the next generation of smart glasses and watches, connected cameras, streamers, and industrial vision and voice systems.

 The new low-power Edge AI chip from Synaptics, as displayed next to a coin for its relative size. 

 5. TimesFM and TabFM transform how businesses work with numbers

 While language models excel with text, business and operational decisions also rely on numbers. TimesFM and TabFM are foundational models engineered specifically to reason over raw numerical distributions — time-series streams (data that changes over time) and structured tabular data (like spreadsheets). Both models deliver accurate predictions out of the box with zero training. They rank at the top of leading public benchmarks in their fields and are available to all Cloud BigQuery users. Today, we are announcing our upcoming integration of these models into Gemini for business . Soon, business owners, analysts, operation leads or coordinators can forecast trends like product sales or hospital bed capacity, based on complex operational tables and millions of rows of data. Sensitive data stays safely within an organization’s perimeter, and people get the answers they need in seconds.

 TimesFM-3's multivariate forecast helps to anticipate sales lift for a business on planned promotion days in the future. 

 6. MedGemma enables innovators to build and deploy health AI applications

 MedGemma , published last week in Nature Medicine , has been downloaded more than 10 million times by more than 65,000 unique innovators. It serves as an open foundation for developers building specialized applications . Developers have adapted it to meet the needs of their local communities, from enabling faster triage in overcrowded clinics to screening for eye disease and cervical cancer .
 As developers fine-tune MedGemma for more specialities and care settings, we’re pushing the frontier of open health AI. Our latest research advances MedGemma with tool use, so it can draw on available health records and other applications clinicians rely on. We’re exploring new modalities like mammography, ultrasound and electrocardiograms. Early signs point to substantial gains in capabilities, such as answering clinical questions and interpreting radiology scans, skin images and pathology slides. With these advances, we hope to expand what innovators can build, bringing effective healthcare to more communities around the world.

 With our research on AMIE , we’re exploring the use of AI in clinical reasoning and conversations, to understand how it could empower clinicians and strengthen the patient-clinician relationship. Our research this year in Nature advanced AMIE’s capabilities beyond initial diagnosis toward long-term disease management, and in Nature Medicine , we showed how it can reason across multimodal data like medical images and lab results.
 Our new study in The Lancet offers a promising look into how its capabilities could come to life in real-world clinical settings. At Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center , 98 patients safely consulted AMIE ahead of urgent care visits, and clinicians reported that the AI summaries helped them prepare in 75% of cases. We’re also advancing AMIE’s multimodal capabilities towards real-time video consultations and have embarked on a nationwide randomized study of AI in real-world virtual care settings in partnership with Included Health .
 AMIE is part of a rigorous research journey going back to our landmark MedPalm paper, and it’s still early days.

 Optimizing Agent Reliability and Tool Calling Efficiency for Chip Design Using NVIDIA NeMo Gym

 Siemens EDA used agentic evaluations to cut agent turns by 66% while raising benchmark scores from 55% to 95%.

 By Joshua Mabry , Chris Wing , Niranjan Sitapure , Kenton DeLathouwer and Ming Ming Zhang

 AI-Generated Summary

 NVIDIA NeMo Gym provides an open evaluation environment that diagnoses failure modes and tracks error propagation across multistage chip design workflows.
 The Siemens Fuse EDA AI Agent used NeMo Gym to evaluate and improve Liberty file generation for standard-cell characterization, increasing the composite verification score from approximately 55% to ~95% across a representative benchmark.
 Agent turns decreased from 155 to 53 and output tokens fell from approximately 81K to 29K after refining skills and Model Context Protocol tool descriptions based on verifier diagnostics.
 A domain-specific verifier checks coverage, validity, relative validation, accuracy, and integrity of final Liberty artifacts, assigning zero reward if any gate fails.
 The same evaluation method applies to engineering agents in EDA, CAE, and other domains by grading final artifacts and optimizing skills through repeated rollouts.

 AI agents offer remarkable productivity gains in complex chip design workflows, but their tendency to generate plausible yet incorrect artifacts makes reliability a major barrier to production adoption. In multistage engineering workflows, an undetected error early in setup can silently propagate through downstream stages and final artifact generation. Evaluating and refining these agents against verified final outputs, rather than isolated intermediate steps, is essential for building trustworthy automation.

 NVIDIA NeMo Gym , an open library for evaluating and improving models and agents using environments, addresses this challenge. The NeMo Gym agentic evaluation environment is designed to diagnose failure modes and track error propagation across complex, multistage workflows. By establishing a domain-specific verifier to inspect final outputs against verified reference artifacts, NeMo Gym enables engineers to trace complete rollout trajectories and identify root causes behind subtle errors.

 This post walks through how NeMo Gym was used to evaluate and improve the reliability of the Siemens Fuse EDA AI Agent when calling characterization tools. The Siemens Fuse team used NeMo Gym to scale up evaluations and verify the resulting Liberty (.lib) files against known references and tracing—both common and rare failures through each rollout. Those findings guided changes to the agent’s skill and Model Context Protocol (MCP) tool descriptions, increasing the measured benchmark composite score from approximately 55% to ~95% across a benchmark of representative standard-cell characterization tasks, while reducing turns and output tokens.

 Siemens’ work provides a practical example for chip design teams and EDA developers on how to leverage the NVIDIA AI software stack and open libraries to improve agent reliability and chip design workflows.

 Automating standard-cell characterization 

 Standard-cell characterization is the process of generating accurate timing, power, and noise models for logic cells across operating conditions. It is foundational to chip design and required whenever a semiconductor foundry issues a new process design kit (PDK). Each new PDK carries SPICE transistor models; design rules; and process, voltage, and temperature (PVT) definitions that connect the manufacturing process to design tools. When a foundry updates a PDK, existing characterization datasets may no longer accurately describe the updated devices. Timing and power models must then be regenerated and validated for every affected cell across combinations of input slew, output load, and PVT conditions.

 The Solido Characterization Suite agent automates this process. The agent orchestrates tools from the broader Solido Characterization Suite through Siemens Fuse EDA AI Agent, which exposes MCP servers and skills to common coding harnesses including Claude Code, Codex, and Cursor.

 MCP interfaces make these accelerated tools accessible to engineering agents, while skills guide their use in characterization workflows. Faster simulation helps agents complete engineering iterations sooner, while NVIDIA NeMo Gym helps developers measure and improve how reliably and efficiently agents orchestrate those tools.

 The Solido Characterization Suite agent must perform tool setup, large-scale SPICE simulation, distributed compute, Liberty file generation, debugging, and final validation (Figure 1). Errors often produce plausible outputs instead of clean failures, leaving incorrect thresholds, missing corners, or incomplete cells hidden. Because these stages depended on one another, an early setup error could propagate into every step that followed. Defining a rigorous evaluation protocol was a key step in preparing the Solido Characterization Suite agent for production workflows.

 Figure 1. Agentic characterization workflow from SPICE inputs through pilot validation, scale-out, Liberty generation, and waveform comparison. Early setup errors propagate to the final library 

 Measuring and improving agent reliability with NeMo Gym 

 Part of the NVIDIA NeMo collection of open libraries for agent specialization and optimization, NeMo Gym integrates with the standard-cell characterization flow inside a controlled evaluation loop (Figure 2). It defines the task, tools, state, and verifier for each rollout so that attempts started from a clean state and produced comparable results. It also records thinking traces, input and output messages, and tool actions.

 This enabled engineers to run the following optimization loop:

 Run baseline rollouts with a versioned task and verifier in a custom NeMo Gym environment

 Inspect trajectories, failed tool calls, and verifier diagnostics

 Identify ambiguous instructions, unproductive actions, and incorrect tool selection

 Refine the agent’s skills and MCP tool descriptions

 Repeat the same tasks under the same evaluation conditions

 Compare verified outcomes and efficiency per successful result

 Figure 2. NeMo Gym checks the Liberty files produced by the Solido Characterization Suite agent and Solido tools, then feeds failure analysis into the next skill and tool-description revision. The entire process is driven by a coding agent with a human in the loop 

 Reward design and artifact verification 

 As the team analyzed agent trajectories, end-to-end evaluation uncovered failures that intermediate checks missed. For example, final Liberty verification exposed missing cells and operating conditions, incorrect slew thresholds, and timing or power values outside tolerance. These findings show why engineering agents must be evaluated against final artifacts rather than individual tool calls.

 To make the work repeatable, the team implemented verifiers that provide a final composite reward score based on the following metrics:

 Coverage : Whether the agent produced every expected cell and PVT corner.

 Validity : Whether the delivered Liberty files are well-formed and usable by the validation tools.

 Relative validation: Whether the output introduced failures beyond those already present in the reference.

 Accuracy : The fraction of expected timing and power values that falls within the defined tolerance.

 Integrity : Whether the characterization workflow produced the complete result rather than reusing, truncating, or reformatting existing values.

 The reward score is defined as:

 \(R=\mathbf{1}\left[\text{Coverage}\right]\times\mathbf{1}\left[\text{Validity}\right]\times\mathbf{1}\left[\text{Relative Validation}\right]\times\mathbf{1}\left[\text{Integrity}\right]\times\frac{X_{\text{tol}}}{X_{\text{total}}}\)

 Here, \(X_{\mathrm{tol}}\) is the number of values in the output that are within tolerance, and \(X_{\mathrm{total}}\) is the total number of output values. Their ratio represents the fraction of output values within tolerance.

 Each indicator \(\mathbf{1}[\cdot]\) equals \(1\) when its corresponding gate passes and \(0\) when it fails. The reward is zero if any gate fails.

 Using this verifier, the team systematically evaluated and tuned the agent’s performance across multiple iterations.

 Optimizing the agent 

 The team used the open source GF180MCU PDK to benchmark the Solido Characterization Suite agent on Liberty-file generation. The dataset includes 229 standard cells across 36 PVT corners, using Solido AFS for SPICE simulation.

 A custom agentic environment was built using NeMo Gym. For each run, the characterization flow was restricted to two cells across 36 PVT corners, as this smaller subset was sufficient for tuning the agentic workflow. Each run took approximately 1.5 to 2 hours, and the team conducted approximately 25 rollouts using Claude Opus 4.8 running in Claude Code as the fixed model and agent harness.

 Across successive evaluation rounds, the team refined the agent’s characterization skills and MCP tool descriptions. To improve tool selection, they simplified overlapping file and shell interfaces and defined tool inputs with explicit JSON schemas, making characterization tools easier for the agent to call.
